analysis.one_liner: Requires websites to remove nonconsensual intimate images, including AI fakes, within 48 hours and criminalizes sharing them.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2024 with cosponsors from both parties, the bill received no committee action or floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly share intimate images of someone without their consent, including computer-generated 'deepfake' nudes, with prison terms of up to two years for depictions of adults and three for minors. It would also require public websites that host user posts to set up a removal process and take down flagged images within 48 hours of a victim's request, with the Federal Trade Commission enforcing the rule. Exemptions cover law enforcement, medical and legal uses, and reporting; broadband providers, email, and services that are not mainly user-posted content are left out entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of nonconsensual intimate images — disproportionately women and minors, and increasingly targets of AI-generated fakes. They would gain a right to get images taken down from covered platforms within 48 hours of a signed request, and publishers would face criminal fines, prison, forfeiture of proceeds, and mandatory restitution.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime for knowingly publishing a nonconsensual intimate image of an adult (up to 2 years' imprisonment) or a minor (up to 3 years), explicitly covering 'deepfakes' that falsely but realistically depict a person, and adds threats to publish as an equally punishable offense.

Requires every covered platform to establish a signed, written notice-and-removal process within one year and to remove flagged images and identical copies within 48 hours, with immunity for platforms that remove in good faith.

Lets courts order forfeiture of proceeds from the violation and mandatory restitution for victims, and directs the FTC to enforce the removal mandate the same way it enforces unfair and deceptive practices, including against nonprofits.
Defines consent narrowly — an affirmative, voluntary authorization — and states that consenting to create an image, or sharing it with one person, is not consent to publish it.

analysis.who_pays: Websites and apps that host user-generated content must build and staff a takedown process within a year, comply with 48-hour removal deadlines, and face FTC enforcement for failures. Individuals who knowingly publish such images face fines, up to two or three years in prison, forfeiture, and restitution.

drawbacks.text: The 48-hour removal deadline, combined with a liability shield for platforms that remove in good faith, creates a strong incentive to take content down first and ask questions later — which can sweep up consensual or lawful images before anyone verifies the claim.

The takedown mandate covers only services that 'primarily' host user-generated content; email and broadband providers are explicitly excluded, so images circulated through those channels fall outside the removal process.
Small platforms face the same one-year compliance and 48-hour removal obligations as the largest companies, a fixed cost that weighs more heavily on them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and one-sided: victims of intimate-image abuse, including deepfake victims who never consented to anything, currently have no fast federal remedy, and this bill gives them both a takedown right and criminal recourse. The main costs are compliance burdens and a real risk of over-removal of lawful content under the 48-hour clock, though a public-concern exception and platform immunity for good-faith action partially hedge that. On balance a well-aimed bill, with the over-removal risk being its most serious design flaw.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was assigned to never took it up, so it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025 with no hearing, no vote, and no law.

narrative.text: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar introduced the bill on July 10, 2024, joined by original cosponsors from both parties (Reps. Dean, Pfluger, Plaskett, Buchanan, and Dingell).
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced.
Twenty members — 8 of 216 House Democrats and 12 of 224 House Republicans — signed on as cosponsors.
The committee took no further action on the bill, and the full action history shows nothing after the initial referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill never brought to a committee markup or a House vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Websites that host user content avoided a 48-hour removal mandate and Federal Trade Commission enforcement, and no one who shares these images gained any new criminal exposure — while victims gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for criminal penalties and mandatory takedowns of nonconsensual intimate images.

for.name: Reps. Dean, Pfluger, Plaskett, Buchanan, and Dingell
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, three Republicans and two Democrats plus a Democratic delegate.

for.name: 12 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Republican sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: a Republican sponsor with original cosponsors from both parties, and 20 cosponsors split 12 Republicans and 8 Democrats; opposition was not recorded votes but committee inaction under a Republican-controlled House.

industries.industry: Social media and user-generated content platforms
industries.note: The bill would require these platforms to build a removal process within a year, take down flagged images within 48 hours, and answer to the FTC for failures — significant compliance costs and penalty exposure. In exchange they get a liability shield for good-faith removals and a clear legal rule; their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against victims' interest in fast takedowns.

These services are explicitly carved out of the 'covered platform' definition, so they bear no takedown duties. The carve-out narrows protection, since images shared through those channels escape the removal process.
